summary: OSPF is a link-state interior gateway protocol. Every router learns the full topology of its area, then independently runs Dijkstra's shortest-path-first algorithm to build its routing table, so all routers converge on consistent loop-free routes.

sections.heading: Link-state idea
sections.body: Each router describes its own links and neighbours in Link State Advertisements (LSAs) and floods them. All routers in an area end up with an identical link-state database (LSDB), then each computes a shortest-path tree rooted at itself (RFC 2328). OSPF uses a single dimensionless cost metric summed along the path; a common convention is cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth.

sections.heading: Neighbour discovery: Hello protocol
sections.body: Routers send Hello packets (to multicast 224.0.0.5, IP protocol 89) at the hello interval (10 s on broadcast links by default). Neighbours must agree on area, hello and dead intervals, and authentication. The dead interval (default 40 s) declares a silent neighbour down.
bullets: Down: no Hello received.
Init: Hello received but our router ID not yet seen in it.
2-Way: bidirectional communication confirmed; DR/BDR election happens here.
ExStart / Exchange: master/slave negotiation, then database descriptions are swapped.
Loading: missing LSAs are requested.
Full: databases are synchronized; the routers are adjacent.

sections.heading: Designated Router
sections.body: On a broadcast segment every router forming a full mesh of adjacencies would flood needlessly. Instead, a Designated Router (DR) and Backup (BDR) are elected by highest priority, then highest router ID; other routers form adjacencies only with the DR and BDR. DR/BDR listen on 224.0.0.6.

sections.heading: Areas
sections.body: A large network is split into areas to limit flooding and SPF scope. Area 0, the backbone, must be contiguous and connect all other areas (virtual links can patch gaps). Area Border Routers (ABRs) summarize routes between areas; ASBRs inject external routes.
bullets: Internal router: all interfaces in one area.
ABR: interfaces in multiple areas.
Backbone router: at least one interface in area 0.
ASBR: redistributes routes from outside the OSPF domain.

sections.heading: LSA types and flooding
bullets: Type 1 Router LSA: a router's links within an area.
Type 2 Network LSA: generated by the DR for a multi-access segment.
Type 3 Summary LSA: inter-area routes from an ABR.
Type 5 AS-external LSA: routes from an ASBR.
LSAs carry sequence numbers and an age; they are refreshed every 30 minutes and expire at 60 minutes.
Flooding is reliable: each LSA is acknowledged.

sections.body: Start with the router itself at cost 0; repeatedly add the unvisited vertex with the lowest cumulative cost and relax its neighbours. The result is a shortest-path tree from which next hops are derived. A topology change triggers a rerun, often throttled to avoid churn.

Changes are flooded immediately and each router recomputes locally, rather than routes propagating hop by hop with counting-to-infinity risks. Features like fast hello and BFD shorten failure detection to sub-second.
Broadcast and NBMA networks elect a DR; point-to-point links do not. Mismatched network types are a common cause of neighbours stuck in a state.

bullets: Stuck in Init: one-way communication; check ACLs and multicast.
Stuck in ExStart/Exchange: usually an MTU mismatch.
No neighbour: mismatched area ID, hello/dead timers, subnet mask, or authentication.
Useful commands: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf database, show ip route ospf.

sections.body: OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) carries IPv6 and runs per link. IS-IS is a similar link-state protocol popular in service-provider backbones.

takeaways: Link-state: flood LSAs, build the same LSDB everywhere, run SPF locally.
Neighbour states: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.
Area 0 is the backbone; ABRs connect areas; a DR/BDR reduces adjacencies on LANs.
Cost is the metric; MTU, timers, and area mismatches break adjacency.
